title: The Gayatri

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hare Krishna, the great mantra, sung in the street. Your line was the name, out loud. Where did you sing? Today, a verse from the Rig Veda, and it's about the sun. Day one hundred eight.

Before dawn, on the steps down to the river at Varanasi, a man stands waist-deep in the water, facing east. He cups water in his hands, and as the first edge of the sun comes up, he lifts it and lets it pour back, and says a few lines under his breath. Far away in Delhi, a teenager is hearing the same lines on a phone, on the way to school. Same words, at the river and on the road, from a hymn far older than anyone saying them. It's called the Gayatri.
screen: `A MAN IN THE RIVER, FACING EAST.` → `THE SAME LINES ON A PHONE.` → `FAR OLDER THAN BOTH OF THEM.`

segments.voice: It comes from the Rig Veda, book three, hymn sixty-two, verse ten. Tradition says it was seen by the sage Vishvamitra. Gayatri is the name of its meter, three lines of eight syllables, and the verse came to be called by the meter's name, and later became honored as a Goddess herself. Here it is, with the words traditionally said before it: Om bhur bhuvah svah, tat savitur varenyam, bhargo devasya dhimahi, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat. The first words name the three worlds: earth, the sky between, and heaven. Then it turns to Savitr, the sun, but not just the ball of fire. Savitr is the sun as the one who stirs things into life, who wakes everything up. We meditate on that radiance, the verse says. And the last line is the heart of it: may it stir, may it light up, our minds. Not give us things. Illuminate how we think. Light, illuminate the mind. Here's something honest to know. Traditions differ on who should chant it. Many hold that it's given at the sacred thread ceremony and chanted by the initiated, with care. Others, including many modern teachers and movements, have opened it to everyone. Both views are held by devout Hindus. So in today's practice, you don't have to say the Sanskrit at all. You can hold its meaning in English, which nobody restricts. The sun rises for everyone.
screen: `RIG VEDA, BOOK THREE.` · `SAVITR, THE SUN THAT STIRS.` · `MAY IT LIGHT UP OUR MINDS.` · `WHO CHANTS IT: TRADITIONS DIFFER.` · then, large: `LIGHT, ILLUMINATE THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one line, held. Sit facing a window if you can, or picture the sun just coming up. Take a few slow breaths from your routine. Now take only the last line, the heart of it. If your tradition welcomes you to chant it, say softly: dhiyo yo nah prachodayat. If not, hold its meaning in English: light, illuminate the mind. Say it once. Then just hold it, the way you'd hold your face toward the morning sun. Say it again when your attention drifts. The bell holds the time.
The Gayatri. A verse from the Rig Veda, to the sun who stirs everything awake, asking it to light up our minds.
Your line: light, illuminate the mind. Tomorrow morning, before your phone, find the light from a window, and give it one line and one breath. Day one hundred eight.

howItsDone: Many Hindus chant the Gayatri at dawn and dusk as part of sandhya worship, often facing the sun and offering water; traditionally it is taught at the upanayana (sacred thread) ceremony, while many modern teachers and movements share it with all.

what a scholar hears: Rig Veda 3.62.10, attributed to Vishvamitra, in gayatri meter; the vyahritis bhur bhuvah svah are prefixed from later Vedic practice; who may chant it has long been debated.

notes: IMPORTANT: The Gayatri is quoted in full in transliteration. Many traditions restrict its chanting to those who have received upanayana; others (e.g. Arya Samaj, many modern teachers) teach it to all. The script presents both views without ranking and offers an English alternative. A Keeper must decide whether the full Sanskrit should be spoken in the app.
Attribution to Vishvamitra and the dating 'three thousand years' (Rig Veda book 3 is among the older family books, c. 1500–1000 BCE). Confirm or soften.

The vyahritis (bhur bhuvah svah) are prefixed in practice (from the Taittiriya Aranyaka / Yajur Veda usage); they are not in RV 3.62.10 itself. Confirm framing 'the three words most people say before it'.
Translation of the last line ('may it stir, may it light up, our minds') is the writer's paraphrase; no pre-1929 translation quoted. Confirm.
